name: Fitness
about: A training session in three phases. Before: the nutrients, hormones and growth brakes you bring to it. During: what the muscle fibres are built for, fast-twitch power or slow-twitch endurance, how they burn fuel, and the strength and mass the genes allow. After: the damage, the inflammation that signals repair, rebuilding and breakdown, tendons and oxidative stress. Genes are placed by Gene Ontology and joined by human genetics from Open Targets.
rule: Gene Ontology stage genes (fibre types from UniProt's curated notes; broad stages only where GTEx shows the gene expressed in skeletal muscle), plus genes with human genetic evidence ≥ 0.5 for a muscle condition (≥ 0.8 for level traits such as grip strength or lean mass)

mechanisms.name: Amino acid uptake and sensing
mechanisms.about: Amino acid transporters and leucine sensing that switch on protein synthesis.

mechanisms.name: Glycogen storage
mechanisms.about: Building the glycogen store the muscle burns in hard efforts.

mechanisms.name: Creatine
mechanisms.about: Making creatine, carrying it into muscle, and charging it to creatine phosphate.

mechanisms.name: Vitamin D signalling
mechanisms.about: The vitamin D receptor and its signal, which muscle strength and fibre size depend on.

mechanisms.name: Testosterone
mechanisms.about: Making testosterone and DHT, and the androgen receptor that carries their signal into muscle.

mechanisms.name: Growth hormone and IGF-1
mechanisms.about: Growth hormone release and signalling, and the IGF-1 receptor pathway it drives in muscle.

mechanisms.name: Growth brakes
mechanisms.about: Myostatin and the other signals that hold muscle growth back, and the follistatins that block them.

mechanisms.name: Growth on load
mechanisms.about: Muscle fibres growing in response to load.

mechanisms.name: Fast fibres
mechanisms.about: The proteins of fast-twitch (type II) fibres: their myosins, troponins, calcium pump and alpha-actinin-3.

mechanisms.name: Slow fibres
mechanisms.about: The proteins of slow-twitch (type I) fibres, and the calcineurin signal that keeps fibres slow.

mechanisms.name: Aerobic capacity
mechanisms.about: Aerobic respiration and building the mitochondrial respiratory chain.

mechanisms.name: Glycogen and glucose burning
mechanisms.about: Breaking glycogen down and burning glucose without oxygen: the fuel for hard efforts.

mechanisms.name: Fat burning
mechanisms.about: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids in the mitochondria: the fuel for long, easy efforts.

mechanisms.name: Lactate and energy sensing
mechanisms.about: Carrying lactate out of working muscle, and AMPK, the sensor that reads the energy drop during exercise.

mechanisms.name: Inflammatory signals
mechanisms.about: IL-6, TNF and IL-1 signalling.

mechanisms.name: Satellite cells and regeneration
mechanisms.about: Satellite cells activating and multiplying, myoblasts fusing, and muscle regrowing.

mechanisms.name: Response to training
mechanisms.about: Genes that respond to muscle activity: PGC-1α and the mitochondria it builds, myokines such as irisin, and the amino acid carriers that feed new protein.

mechanisms.name: mTOR and protein synthesis
mechanisms.about: The mTOR signal that turns load, amino acids and IGF-1 into new muscle protein.

mechanisms.name: Atrophy
mechanisms.about: Muscle wasting: the atrogenes and the signals that switch them on.

mechanisms.name: Cortisol response
mechanisms.about: Muscle's response to glucocorticoids, which push protein breakdown.

mechanisms.name: Tendons and collagen
mechanisms.about: Building tendons and laying down collagen fibrils.

mechanisms.name: Antioxidant enzymes
mechanisms.about: Enzymes that neutralise oxidants: superoxide dismutases, catalase, peroxidases and peroxiredoxins.

disease_explain: Human genetics (Open Targets) ties these genes to muscle strength, mass, damage or recovery, but Gene Ontology places them in none of the stages yet. Most are GWAS loci near a gene whose role in muscle is still unclear.

organs.name: Nutrient processing
organs.about: Taking up amino acids and sensing leucine, storing glycogen, making and loading creatine, and vitamin D signalling.

organs.name: Testosterone and growth hormone
organs.about: Making testosterone and the muscle's androgen receptor; growth hormone and the IGF-1 signal it drives.

organs.name: Growth brakes and boosters
organs.about: Myostatin and the signals that set how much muscle the body allows, and the drive to grow when loaded.

organs.name: Fast-twitch: power
organs.about: Type II fibres: explosive force for sprinting and lifting, fuelled by creatine phosphate and glycogen, tiring fast.

organs.name: Slow-twitch: endurance
organs.about: Type I fibres: steady work on oxygen, rich in mitochondria and capillaries, slow to tire.

organs.name: Fuel during effort
organs.about: Breaking down glycogen and glucose, burning fat, clearing lactate, and the energy sensor AMPK.

organs.name: Strength and mass potential
organs.about: Genes that human genetics ties to grip strength and lean mass: the ceiling the genes set, before training.

organs.name: Muscle damage
organs.about: How much muscle leaks into the blood after hard work (creatine kinase), and strains and rhabdomyolysis.

organs.name: Inflammation
organs.about: The repair signal: IL-6 from working muscle drives adaptation, while lasting TNF and IL-1 drive breakdown.

organs.name: Rebuilding and adaptation
organs.about: Satellite stem cells waking, multiplying and fusing into fibres, mTOR driving protein synthesis, and PGC-1α building mitochondria: how the muscle adapts to the training.

organs.name: Breakdown
organs.about: Atrophy: atrogin-1 and MuRF1 tagging protein for removal, cortisol, and the loss of muscle with age.

organs.name: Tendons and connective tissue
organs.about: Collagen fibrils and tendon building: what carries the force from muscle to bone, and its injuries.

organs.name: Oxidative stress
organs.about: Clearing the free radicals that hard exercise makes: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidases.
